opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly I think we're still in the early days of figuring out what long context is really for. When we first pushed context windows out to hundreds of thousands and then millions of tokens, a lot of the initial demos were sort of "needle in a haystack": can the model find this one fact buried in a huge document? That's useful as a sanity check, but it's not really the interesting part.

What I find more exciting is that long context changes how you can think about adapting a model to a task. Traditionally, if you wanted a model to know about your codebase, or your company's documents, or a new language, you'd think about fine-tuning, or retrieval systems with a lot of engineering around them. With a very long context, you can just put the whole thing in. You give it the entire repository, or hours of video, or a grammar book for a low-resource language, and the model learns in context. It's a kind of learning that happens at inference time, and I think that's quite profound from a research perspective.

Over the next few years, I'd expect a few things. One is that it becomes much more of a default rather than a special feature. People won't think "do I need long context?" They'll just bring their whole working set: all their documents, their full history with an assistant, the whole project. Second, I think it's going to be really important for agents. If a model is going to act over long horizons, taking many steps, using tools, coming back to a task over days, it needs something like a working memory, and long context is a natural way to provide that, perhaps combined with other memory mechanisms.

There are still real challenges. Cost and latency matter. Processing millions of tokens isn't free, so there's a lot of work on making attention and serving more efficient, caching, and so on. And there's a question of quality: it's not enough to fit the tokens in, the model has to actually reason across all of them, not just retrieve. That's where I think a lot of the research effort is going.

But if I had to bet, I'd say that in a few years we'll look back and find it a bit strange that we ever had to carefully chop information into small pieces to fit it into a model. Long context, plus multimodality, video, audio, code, will just be how people interact with these systems.

r001.rationale: The response says long context may become a default over the next few years, but does not state that deployment at scale is technologically close or conditional on a compelling use case.

r002.rationale: It gives no forecast of context windows growing by roughly an order of magnitude within one or two years.

r003.rationale: It mentions combining long context with other memory mechanisms, but does not propose hierarchical memory with RAG to support extremely long context at deployment scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think long context is one of those things where the first reaction people had was, "Okay, a million tokens, that's a nice demo, you can put a whole book in there." But honestly, I think the demos undersell what's actually going to happen, because the interesting part isn't the size, it's what the size unlocks in terms of how you interact with the model.

Let me break it down a bit. Right now, the dominant pattern is retrieval: you have a big corpus, you chunk it, you embed it, you pull a few relevant pieces, and you stuff those into the prompt. That works, but it's lossy. The model never actually sees the whole thing, and you're relying on a separate system to guess what matters. With very long context, you can skip a lot of that. You just give the model the entire codebase, or every email thread on a project, or all the transcripts from a set of meetings, and let it reason over all of it at once. And what we've seen is that the model does things you simply can't do with retrieval, like noticing that something on page three contradicts something on page four hundred.

So the first wave, which is already happening, is that kind of "bring everything" use case. Developers putting whole repositories in. Analysts dumping entire document collections. And I think that gets much more common as the cost comes down, because today the main blocker isn't capability, it's that processing millions of tokens on every call is expensive and slow.

The second thing, which I'm personally more excited about, is multimodality in long context. Text is actually quite compact. An hour of video is a very large number of tokens. So a million or ten million tokens is the difference between "the model can look at a clip" and "the model watched the whole film and can tell you when the character changed their jacket." Same for audio, for long sensor streams, for a robot's history of what it saw during the day. I think that's where long context stops being a feature and starts being a requirement, because there's no good way to retrieve over video the way you can over text.

And then the third thing, which is maybe a few years out, is a kind of personalization or memory. Imagine the context window just contains everything you've ever done with the model: every conversation, every document you've shared, every correction you made. Instead of fine-tuning on you, the model just has you in context. That's a very different way of thinking about memory, and it's very appealing because it's transparent, you can inspect it, you can delete things. The challenge is that it has to be fast and cheap enough to be always on, and the model has to actually use the information well, not just technically have access to it. That second part is still an active research question. It's one thing to pass a needle-in-a-haystack test, it's another to synthesize across millions of tokens the way a person who's known you for years would.

So if I had to summarize: I think very long context becomes mostly invisible. People won't talk about it as "long context," they'll just notice that the model knows their whole codebase, has seen the whole video, remembers the last six months. And the research work is less about pushing the raw number higher and more about making it cheap, and making the model actually good at using all of that information, not just storing it.

r001.rationale: The response says long-context use is already emerging and may become more common as costs fall, but it does not state that deployment at scale is technologically close, conditional on a compelling use case.

r002.rationale: It gives no prediction that common context windows will grow by roughly an order of magnitude within one or two years.

r003.rationale: It discusses retrieval and personalization separately, but does not propose combining hierarchical memory with retrieval-augmented generation for deployment at scale.

astra-6.text:
I think long context will become much more natural to use, to the point where people may not think about context windows at all. You’ll want to give the model a whole codebase, or a collection of documents, or a long video, and then have a conversation about it. You shouldn’t have to decide in advance which little pieces are relevant.

But there’s a distinction between being able to put a lot of information into the context and actually using it well. Can the model connect something at the beginning with something much later? Can it find the relevant detail when there are many similar details? Those capabilities matter as much as the number of tokens.

And then there’s cost and latency. If you’re repeatedly asking questions about the same material, you’d like to reuse the computation. As that becomes more efficient, I think we’ll see a shift from these short, isolated interactions toward systems that have much more of the context of what you’re working on. Retrieval will still be useful, but users will have to do less of that selection themselves.

r001.rationale: The response discusses long context becoming more natural and more efficient, but does not say deployment at scale is technologically close or condition that on a compelling use case.

r002.rationale: It gives no prediction about context-window growth by an order of magnitude or a one-to-two-year timeframe.

r003.rationale: It says retrieval will remain useful, but does not propose combining hierarchical memory with retrieval-augmented generation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think long context changes how we interact with these models. Instead of trying to squeeze everything into a short question, you can give the model the material you’re working with—a codebase, a collection of documents, a long video—and then have a conversation about it.

But the important distinction is between being able to put information into the context and the model actually using it well. If the relevant detail is somewhere in hours of video or thousands of pages, can it find that detail, connect it to something else, and give you a reliable answer? That’s the capability we need to keep improving.

I suspect it will become fairly invisible to users. You won’t necessarily think about how many tokens you have. You’ll expect the assistant to have the context it needs. And then the practical questions are cost, latency, and deciding what information should be available to it. Having a very large window is useful, but making that feel fast and natural is what will drive widespread use.

r001.rationale: The response says very large context windows are useful and that making them fast and natural will drive adoption, but it does not say deployment at scale is technologically close or condition that on a compelling use case.

r002.rationale: It predicts context will become less visible to users, but gives no estimate of window growth or timeframe.

r003.rationale: It discusses finding and using information in long contexts, but does not propose hierarchical memory combined with retrieval-augmented generation.
